problems.memo_sentence: The authors introduce Q-CHOP, a quantum constrained Hamiltonian optimization algorithm that keeps a constraint Hamiltonian always on so that the system evolves entirely within the feasible subspace, while an objective Hamiltonian is slowly rotated to map a worst feasible state into a best feasible state along an adiabatic path.
problems.source_evidence: “We also discuss a relaxation of the requirement to identify and prepare a worst feasible state.” / “We leave the investigation of Q-CHOP with arbitrary-feasible-state initialization to future work.”
problems.explanation: The memo presents the worst-feasible-state initialization as a settled part of the algorithm, but the paper explicitly says this is relaxed only in discussion and that the arbitrary-feasible-state version is left for future work. That limitation materially changes the scope of the method.

problems.memo_sentence: Across a wide range of benchmark problems—graph problems like maximum independent set and directed minimum dominating set, knapsack, combinatorial auctions, and a bond ETF basket optimization use case—the simulations indicate that Q-CHOP consistently achieves higher in-constraint approximation ratios and substantially higher probabilities of reaching optimal or near-optimal solutions than a standard penalty-based adiabatic annealing baseline.
problems.source_evidence: “we provide strong numerical evidence that Q-CHOP outperforms the standard adiabatic algorithm for a variety of textbook and industrial constrained optimization problems.” / “The performance of Q-CHOP and the SQAA for the knapsack problem is more variable…” / “There is no longer a clean separation between Q-CHOP and the SQAA in how their near-optimal-state probability grows with the quantum runtime T, but typical growth for Q-CHOP is more favorable than that for the SQAA.”
problems.explanation: The memo turns a broad, qualified performance claim into a universal one. The paper itself notes variability, plateau behavior, and in the ETF case the absence of a clean separation in growth trends, so “consistently” and “substantially” overstate the evidence.

problems.memo_sentence: The authors acknowledge that Q-CHOP can struggle or fail on problem classes where the feasible subspace is weakly connected or disconnected under the objective-induced mixer, potentially making it impossible to reach good or optimal solutions if they lie in different connected components from the chosen worst feasible state.
problems.source_evidence: “these free parameters do not allow Q-CHOP to solve arbitrary constrained optimization problems, most notably those whose feasible subspace is loosely connected—or disconnected entirely—by the mixer that Q-CHOP constructs out of the objective Hamiltonian” / “Q-CHOP may be unable to produce optimal—or even good—solutions entirely, if these solutions lie in different connected components than that of the worst feasible state.”
problems.explanation: This is a central limitation in the paper, but the memo does not reflect it in the main method/result summaries. The omission matters because it qualifies the scope of Q-CHOP’s applicability.

problems.memo_sentence: They also note an equivalence between Q-CHOP and a prior non-Abelian adiabatic mixing algorithm on MIS, and interpret one additional term in their construction as an approximate counterdiabatic driving component that may help performance.
problems.source_evidence: “In the case of MIS, we show in Appendix A that Q-CHOP is equivalent to the specialized algorithm based on non-Abelian adiabatic mixing proposed in Ref. [32]” / “the addition of ∂tθSy can be identified with approximate counterdiabatic driving (see Appendix B)”
problems.explanation: The equivalence to the non-Abelian adiabatic mixing algorithm is explicitly attributed to Ref. [32], not presented as a new result of this paper. The memo attributes the prior algorithmic equivalence to the paper itself without noting that it is a comparison to an earlier specialized method.
